title: Glassblowing made Roman glass so cheap a cup could cost one copper coin

cover.alt: A glowing orange gather of molten glass hangs from the end of a dark blowpipe, just lowered into a round mould.

body: Early Roman glass was mostly cast, slow work that left thick-walled vessels needing a lot of finishing, so glass stayed an **expensive, high-status** material. Blowing a bubble of molten glass on the end of a pipe changed that. The walls could be much thinner, so each vessel took less glass, and the work was quicker, with far less finishing. By the mid-1st century AD, the geographer Strabo noted that a glass drinking cup could be bought for **a copper coin**.

slides.alt: A glowing gather of molten glass on the end of a blowpipe is lowered into a dark mould and slowly swells into a large round orange bubble.
slides.caption: At a glassworks in Eswatini, a gather of molten glass on a blowpipe is lowered into a mould and blown. It swells into a glowing bubble that will become the bowl of a wine glass.

slides.heading: From rare to everywhere
slides.text: At the start of the 1st century AD there was still no Latin word for glass. By the late 1st century, blowing had largely replaced the older methods, and by the early 2nd century glass objects turned up in homes of every kind across the Roman world.

slides.prompt: Cheap cups weren’t the only new thing in Rome’s glass boom. What else did glassmakers make for the first time?
slides.answer: Window glass, and glass tiles for mosaics
slides.detail: As furnaces improved enough to melt glass fully, the first glass mosaic tiles and the first window glass followed.

slides.question: Why did blown glass cost less than the cast glass before it?
options: It was made from cheaper sand
It needed no furnace at all
It was shipped in from China
slides.explanation: Blown vessels had much thinner walls, so each took less glass, and blowing was quicker, with far less finishing to do.
